A particular feature is being examined across two populations to determine if the distribution of the feature depends on the population. The feature can take three values, $A_{1}$, $A_{2}$, and $A_{3}$.

A sample of $120$ individuals from the first population and $80$ individuals from the second population is carried out. The following contingency table reports the observed frequencies.

|  | $A_{1}$ | $A_{2}$ | $A_{3}$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Population 1 | $O_{11} = 30$ | $O_{12} = 36$ | $O_{13} = 54$ |
| Population 2 | $O_{21} = 40$ | $O_{22} = 18$ | $O_{23} = 22$ |

A chi-square test for homogeneity is conducted at the $2.5%$ significance level with the following null and alternative hypotheses:

- $H_{0}$: The distribution of the feature is the same across both populations
- $H_{1}$: The distribution of the feature is not the same across both populations

The table below gives the values of $w$ that satisfy $P(W \ge w) = p$, where $W∼χ^{2}(ν)$.

| $k∖p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $2$ | $4.605$ | $5.991$ | $7.378$ | $9.210$ |
| $3$ | $6.251$ | $7.815$ | $9.348$ | $11.345$ |
| $4$ | $7.779$ | $9.488$ | $11.143$ | $13.277$ |

Using this information, select the options that make the following statements true.

Rounded to one decimal place, the test statistic is approximately
{{field-1}}.

The number of degrees of freedom for this test is $ν =$ {{field-2}}.

At the $2.5%$ significance level, there is {{field-3}} evidence to reject the null hypothesis.
